newsitem.title: USA: Lott holds key as Senate votes on chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Lott holds key as Senate votes on chemical treaty.

text.p: The U.S. Senate headed for a series of votes on Thursday on a treaty outlawing chemical weapons, with Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott holding the key to ratification.

As President Bill Clinton lobbied hard for Senate approval of the Chemical Weapons Convention, Lott continued to voice concerns about provisions he said could lead to sensitive chemical technology going to "rogue" states.
He is expected to announced some time on Thursday whether talks with administration officials have yielded sufficient assurances that this will not happen, allowing him to vote for the treaty.

Both supporters and opponents say that a decision by Lott to vote for the pact would influence undecided Republicans, likely providing enough votes to give it the required two-thirds majority needed for consent to ratification.

As the Senate opened debate on Wednesday, Clinton stepped up his fight for the treaty with a White House ceremony at which his Republican presidential election opponent, Bob Dole, announced his support, joined by Retired Gen. Colin Powell, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Treaty supporters hailed Dole's announcement -- a reversal of his position last September during the heat of the election campaign -- but a Republican Senate aide said it had not resulted in any loss of potential votes against the treaty.

The Senate session on Thursday will include a rare closed meeting to discuss sensitive security issues before senators begin debating and voting on five provisions that treaty supporters want to strip out of the ratification resolution.
Four are being called "killer" amendments because if they are not removed from the resolution the United States would be prevented from joining 70 other countries in ratifying the treaty.

One of the "killers" would require changes in the treaty to eliminate provisions critics say would require the United States to trade sensitive chemical technology that could wind up in the hands of countries such as Iran or Libya -- a charge denied by treaty supporters.

Lott has called these provisions major flaws in the treaty. But he said late on Wednesday he was still in talks with administration officials on the issue and appeared to be seeking a way out of the perceived problem short of insisting on renegotiating the treaty.
